Visual field impairment
A condition characterized by defects in the visual field that may be progressive or clinically indicated.

Progressive eye condition
An ocular disorder that worsens over time, requiring specific assessment protocols.

Confrontation test
An inexact screening method used to detect visual field defects when no clinical indication of impairment or progressive condition exists.

Formal perimetry-based assessment
A rigorous evaluation procedure required for individuals with suspected or confirmed visual field defects.

Monocular automated static perimetry
The minimum baseline standard for visual field assessments, used to confirm compliance when no defect is detected.

Binocular Esterman visual field
A specific assessment protocol required for subjects with significant field defects or progressive eye conditions.

Humphrey visual field analyser
A device classically used to administer the binocular Esterman visual field test.

Medmont binocular VF
An alternative device capable of producing a level map mode printout equivalent to the standard Esterman chart.

Treating optometrist
A healthcare professional responsible for determining whether a patient should wear corrective lenses during testing.<SEP>A medical professional who assesses and certifies a person's vision status according to specific standards.

Treating ophthalmologist
A healthcare professional responsible for determining whether a patient should wear corrective lenses during testing.

Fixation monitoring
A procedure that must be performed and recorded on the test to ensure subject compliance.

False-positive score
A metric representing the percentage of incorrect positive results in a visual field test, which must not exceed 20 per cent for licensing reliability.

Visual field defect
Any person with a visual field defect or suspected of having one must undergo a formal perimetry-based assessment.

Visual field assessments
This method serves as the minimum baseline standard for visual field assessments; if it shows no defect, the standard is confirmed.

Significant field defect
Subjects with a significant field defect or progressive eye condition require a binocular Esterman visual field for assessment.

Corrective lenses
The treating optometrist determines whether it is appropriate for a person to wear their normal corrective lenses during testing.<SEP>Eyewear used to improve vision and allow a person with suboptimal uncorrected visual acuity to meet driving standards.

Test
Fixation monitoring must be performed and recorded on the test to ensure validity.

Alternative devices
Alternative devices must have the ability to monitor fixation in order to be considered for use.

Esterman binocular chart
For an Esterman binocular chart to be considered reliable for licensing, the false-positive score must not exceed 20 per cent.

Diplopia
A visual condition characterized by double vision, excluding minor forms.<SEP>A condition characterized by double vision, excluding physiological diplopia.<SEP>A medical condition characterized by double vision, which is evaluated for its impact on driving fitness.

Driving
The act of operating a vehicle, which individuals with significant diplopia are generally unfit to perform.<SEP>The activity that may be restricted due to progressive eye conditions.

Optometrist
A healthcare professional specializing in eye care who can assess patients experiencing diplopia.<SEP>A healthcare professional who recommends how lenses should be worn for orthokeratology therapy.<SEP>A healthcare professional who may refer a person for further assessment if they do not meet visual acuity standards.<SEP>A professional who assesses longstanding field defects for conditional licence consideration.

Ophthalmologist
An ophthalmologist is a medical doctor specializing in the diagnosis and treatment of eye diseases, serving as a key healthcare professional for assessing patients experiencing diplopia. This specialist evaluates eye health and vision to determine if an individual meets specific visual acuity standards or licensing requirements, often certifying a person's vision status according to established criteria.

In the context of driving, an ophthalmologist assesses longstanding field defects for conditional licence consideration and provides critical information regarding a driver's visual capabilities to the licensing authority. They recommend how lenses should be worn for orthokeratology therapy when necessary and may refer a person for further assessment if they do not meet required visual standards. Ultimately, this medical specialist plays a pivotal role in evaluating eye health and vision to ensure drivers satisfy the legal and safety prerequisites for operating a vehicle.

Occluder
A device used to manage diplopia by covering one eye, requiring a three-month non-driving period for re-establishment of depth perception.

Depth Perception
The ability to perceive the world in three dimensions, which must be re-established after a non-driving period following diplopia management with an occluder.

Commercial Standards
Standards applicable to drivers of heavy vehicles, public passenger vehicles, or those requiring a dangerous goods driver licence.

Unconditional Licence
A driving licence that is not subject to conditions based on visual fitness criteria.<SEP>A type of official permission or authorization that is subject to specific fitness criteria regarding vision.<SEP>A type of license that can be held by individuals meeting specific criteria, excluding those with visual field defects.<SEP>A type of driving licence that a person is not fit to hold if they are monocular.<SEP>A type of driving licence that can be held without specific restrictions, subject to fitness criteria.

Conditional Licence
Conditional Licence refers to a specialized form of driving authorization issued by the driver licensing authority, designed for both private and commercial vehicle operators who possess specific medical conditions affecting their vision. Unlike standard permits, this licence is granted subject to strict conditions and monitoring requirements that integrate the nature of the driving task with the individual's medical status, often necessitating adherence to particular visual acuity standards met through corrective measures such as orthokeratology therapy or regular use of lenses.

The administration of a Conditional Licence involves rigorous oversight mechanisms, typically requiring periodic review cycles ranging from annual to biennial intervals depending on the specific criteria and risk assessment. These reviews are not merely administrative but are critical for ensuring that the driver continues to meet the necessary visual benchmarks throughout their tenure. Consequently, the licence may be granted, modified, or revoked based on the outcomes of these evaluations, which serve as a dynamic feedback loop between the regulatory body and the driver's ongoing health status.

In essence, this permit represents a balanced approach to public safety and mobility, allowing individuals with specific visual impairments to operate vehicles while maintaining strict accountability through continuous medical monitoring and conditional restrictions tailored to their unique circumstances.

Driver Licensing Authority
The Driver Licensing Authority is the government body primarily responsible for evaluating, issuing, renewing, suspending, or cancelling a person's driver licence and conditional licence. This entity manages applications for conditional licences by assessing the nature of driving tasks in conjunction with specific medical conditions to determine eligibility. A core function involves reviewing driver fitness, which includes assessing patients with visual field defects based on established visual acuity standards.

Beyond routine licensing, the Authority handles exceptional cases by referring them for further medical specialist opinion when necessary. It is also tasked with reviewing conditional licences periodically; while some descriptions indicate an annual review cycle, others specify a two-year interval, suggesting a structured but potentially variable monitoring process depending on individual circumstances. Ultimately, the Driver Licensing Authority serves as the central authority ensuring that driving privileges are granted only to those who meet rigorous safety and medical requirements.

Treating Optometrist
A medical professional who provides information regarding a person's visual field to the licensing authority.<SEP>A medical professional who assesses and certifies visual acuity for driving license eligibility.<SEP>A medical professional who provides information regarding a driver's visual capabilities to the licensing authority.<SEP>A medical professional who provides information regarding a person's visual acuity and field to the driver licensing authority.

Treating Ophthalmologist
A medical professional who provides information regarding a person's visual field to the licensing authority.

Visual Field Defect
Any defect in the visual field that renders a person unfit to hold an unconditional licence.

Binocular Visual Field
The combined visual field of both eyes, required to have an extent of at least 140 degrees within 10 degrees above and below the horizontal midline.<SEP>The extent of vision available to both eyes simultaneously, measured in degrees relative to the horizontal midline.

Scotoma
A type of significant visual field loss that may impede driving performance.<SEP>A localized area of visual field loss or blind spot.

Hemianopia
A type of significant visual field loss that may impede driving performance.<SEP>A condition characterized by loss of vision in one half of the visual field.<SEP>A condition characterized by the loss of vision in half of the visual field.

Quadrantanopia
A type of significant visual field loss that may impede driving performance.<SEP>A condition characterized by loss of vision in one quarter of the visual field.<SEP>A type of visual field reduction resulting from neurological conditions or injuries.<SEP>A condition characterized by the loss of vision in one quarter of the visual field.

Visual Acuity
The sharpness of vision in the remaining eye, required to be 6/9 or better with or without correction for monocular drivers.<SEP>A person's clarity of vision, measured with or without glasses or contact lenses.<SEP>Visual acuity refers to the sharpness or clarity of vision, and evidence suggests that reduced levels increase motor vehicle crash risk, though this is challenging to identify precisely.<SEP>The sharpness of vision, a critical factor in detecting objects while driving.<SEP>A main aspect of vision being assessed in the chapter.<SEP>The measure of the sharpness of vision, specifically assessed in its uncorrected state for licensing purposes.<SEP>The sharpness of vision in the remaining eye, which must be 6/9 or better with or without correction.

Monocular Vision
The state of having only one functional eye, which renders a person unfit to hold an unconditional licence.<SEP>The state of having vision with only one eye, resulting in reduced visual fields due to nasal obstruction and lack of stereoscopic vision.

Significant Visual Field Loss
A person is not fit for a conditional licence if they have significant visual field loss (such as scotoma, hemianopia, or quadrantanopia) likely to impede driving performance.<SEP>For a conditional licence based on monocular vision, there must be no other significant visual field loss likely to impede driving performance.

Visual Field Loss
For a conditional licence based on binocular vision, the visual field loss must be static and unlikely to progress rapidly.

Visual Field
For a conditional licence based on monocular vision, the visual field in the remaining eye must have a horizontal extent of at least 140 degrees within 10 degrees above and below the horizontal midline.<SEP>The extent of the area around a person that is visible at any one time, specifically requiring a horizontal extent of at least 140 degrees within 10 degrees above and below the horizontal midline.

Commercial standards
Standards applicable to drivers of heavy vehicles, public passenger vehicles, or those requiring a dangerous goods driver licence.<SEP>A set of requirements for drivers of heavy vehicles, public passenger vehicles, or those requiring a dangerous goods driver licence.

Unconditional licence
A type of driving licence that can be held by a person who meets specific fitness criteria.<SEP>A driving licence that is held without conditions, subject to specific visual acuity limits for the holder.

Conditional licence
A type of driving licence subject to conditions, which a person is not fit to hold if they experience certain visual impairments.<SEP>A driving licence that may be granted by the driver licensing authority subject to periodic review based on meeting specific visual standards.<SEP>A driving permit that requires assessment of visual field defects by an optometrist or ophthalmologist.

Physiological diplopia
A form of diplopia that is considered normal or inherent and does not disqualify a person from holding a licence.

Central fixation
The point in the visual field where an object is directly viewed, used as a reference for measuring diplopia.

Orthokeratology
A therapeutic approach involving the use of rigid gas-permeable contact lenses worn overnight to reshape the cornea of the eye.

Rigid Gas-Permeable Contact Lenses
Specialized contact lenses used in orthokeratology therapy that are worn overnight to reshape the cornea.

Cornea
The transparent front part of the eye that is reshaped by orthokeratology therapy.

Visual Refractive Error
A condition corrected by orthokeratology therapy, providing effective visual correction once the lenses are removed.

Private Vehicle Drivers
Individuals who may obtain a conditional licence to drive without normal correcting lenses if they meet visual acuity standards using orthokeratology therapy.

Commercial Vehicle Drivers
Individuals who may obtain a conditional licence to drive without normal correcting lenses if they meet visual acuity standards using orthokeratology therapy.<SEP>Drivers operating trucks, buses, or other commercial vehicles who face no flexibility regarding visual field assessments.

Medical Specialist Opinion
A formal assessment or recommendation provided by a medical specialist regarding an individual's condition or eligibility.

Part A section 3.3.7
A specific section within Part A of the document that details the role of independent experts and panels.

Visual Acuity Standard
A benchmark or requirement for clear vision that must be met for driving.<SEP>The required level of visual clarity that drivers with nystagmus must satisfy to be considered fit to drive.

Orthokeratology Therapy
A therapeutic treatment used to maintain visual acuity standards.<SEP>A therapy used to meet the visual standard for a conditional license, as referenced in section 10.2.7.

Correcting Lenses
Eyewear devices used to enable individuals to meet visual acuity standards when orthokeratology therapy is insufficient.

Health Professional
An individual required to provide details of medical criteria not met, evidence of criteria met, proposed conditions, and monitoring requirements for the issuance of a conditional licence.

Driver Licence
A document that can be issued, renewed, suspended, or cancelled, including a conditional licence.

Health
A relevant factor considered in licensing decisions regarding fitness to drive.

Driving Performance
A relevant factor considered in licensing decisions regarding fitness to drive.<SEP>The ability to operate a vehicle safely and effectively.<SEP>The ability to operate a vehicle safely, which may be impeded by significant visual field loss.

Medical Criteria
Standards or requirements related to health that must be met for driving eligibility.

Hearing Impairment
A medical condition that may affect fitness to drive when combined with other conditions.

Visual Impairment
A medical condition that may affect fitness to drive when combined with other conditions.

Cognitive Impairment
A medical condition that may affect fitness to drive when combined with other conditions.

Older Drivers and Age-Related Changes
A section referenced regarding age-related factors affecting driving fitness.

Multiple Medical Conditions
A section referenced regarding the combination of concurrent medical conditions affecting fitness to drive.

Fitness to Drive
Hearing impairment may combine with other medical conditions to affect fitness to drive.<SEP>The assessment of a person's ability and safety to operate a vehicle.

Nystagmus
A visual condition that may reduce visual acuity and requires assessment regarding fitness to drive.

Drivers
Individuals who must meet specific visual acuity standards when they have nystagmus.<SEP>Individuals operating vehicles, categorized as either private or commercial, who are subject to potential standards regarding color vision.

Congenital Nystagmus
A form of nystagmus present from birth, which may involve coping strategies compatible with safe driving.

Appropriate Specialist
A qualified professional who should conduct individual assessments for those with congenital nystagmus.

Visual Fields
The visual field is a concept regarding the extent of space visible to an observer, which is noted as having incomplete evidence regarding its relationship to crash risk.<SEP>The extent of visual perception in all directions from the point of fixation, often affected by disorders of vision.<SEP>The extent of the area visible to an observer, important for detecting hazards.<SEP>A main aspect of vision being assessed in the chapter.

Motor Vehicle Crash Risk
This concept represents the likelihood of a vehicle accident, which is the primary outcome being investigated in relation to visual impairment factors.

Licensing Standards
These are established criteria used to determine if a driver is legally permitted to operate a vehicle, and current evidence mostly covers drivers who already meet these standards.

Red Colour-Deficient Vision
A specific type of visual impairment characterized by difficulty distinguishing red colors, which presents challenges in detecting traffic signals like red lights.

Road Engineering
Refers to the design and construction of roads and infrastructure, with significant improvements noted that may allow individuals with certain visual deficiencies to compensate while driving.

Driver licensing authority
The governmental body responsible for evaluating and granting driving licences based on medical and visual criteria.

Visual acuity
The clarity of vision measured as a ratio, such as 6/9 or 6/18, which determines fitness to hold certain types of driving licences.

Orthokeratology therapy
A treatment method referenced for meeting visual standards without corrective lenses, involving the use of contact lenses.

Central Loss
A visual field defect defined as an extension of hemianopia or quadrantanopia involving more than three missed points.

Real-World Driving Environment
The practical context of driving where drivers move their eyes freely and operate under variable conditions.

Kinetic Fields
A method of measuring visual fields conducted on a Goldman device.

Esterman Visual Fields
A method of measuring visual fields that can be conducted binocularly without fixation monitoring, often referred to as roving Esterman.

Roving Esterman
A specific type of Esterman visual field test requiring two consecutive tests with no more than one false-positive allowed.

Numeric Field Format
The format in which roving Esterman visual fields should be printed or sent for an opinion.

Contrast Sensitivity
A factor considered by driver licensing authorities when assessing patients with visual field defects.

Glare Susceptibility
A factor considered by driver licensing authorities when assessing patients with visual field defects.

Medical History
Information regarding the duration and prognosis of a condition, whether it is progressive, the rate of progression or deterioration, and the effectiveness of treatment or management.

Driving Record
The history of driving behavior before and after the occurrence of a visual defect.

Nature of Driving Task
Factors such as vehicle type, road conditions, distances to be travelled, and concomitant medical conditions like cognitive impairment or neck rotation issues.

Visual fields
A measure of the extent of peripheral (side) vision used for assessing driving awareness and safety.

Normal visual field
Defined as 60 degrees nasally, 100 degrees temporally, 75 degrees inferiorly, and 60 degrees superiorly.

Binocular field
Extends the horizontal extent from 160 to 200 degrees, with a central 120 degrees overlapping for stereopsis.

Stroke
A neurological condition that can reduce visual fields.<SEP>A neurological condition where vision is one of several functional outcomes assessed for driving fitness.

Multiple sclerosis
A neurological condition that can reduce visual fields.

Glaucoma
An ocular disease that can reduce visual fields.<SEP>An example of a progressive eye condition mentioned in the text.<SEP>A progressive eye condition that is more common in older people and requires regular monitoring for driving.

Hemionopia
A type of visual field reduction resulting from neurological conditions or injuries.

Monocularity
A type of visual field reduction resulting from neurological conditions or injuries.

Fovea area
The central part of the eye where information is identified after being alerted by peripheral vision.

Driver
Assists the driver in being aware of the total driving environment before central focus is applied.

Peripheral vision
Assists the driver in being aware of the total driving environment before central focus is applied.

Peripheral vision loss
Incomplete peripheral vision loss allows awareness through adaptation, while full impairment decreases safety.

Farmer
An individual requiring a commercial vehicle licence for the occasional use of a heavy vehicle.

Interstate Multiple Combination Vehicle Driver
A driver whose licence status differs from that of a farmer due to the nature of their driving task.

Examining Health Professional
The professional responsible for examining persons and providing advice to the driver licensing authority regarding medical conditions.

Patient
An individual whose condition may affect their ability to drive and who has a legal obligation to notify authorities.

Practical Driver Assessment
A method used to assess the ability to process visual information and evaluate driving effects, though noted as not safe or reliable for assessing disorders of vision.

Disorders of Vision
Conditions affecting vision that may impact driving capabilities.

Emergency Situations
Critical driving scenarios where a driver's response is evaluated but cannot be reliably determined through practical assessments.

Environmental Conditions
Various external factors present during driving that influence the assessment of visual disorders.

Visual Field Tests
Testing procedures used to gain information about adaptation to visual field defects, considered more reliable than practical assessments for this purpose.

Esterman
A specific type of visual field test mentioned as a method for gaining information about adaptation to visual field defects.

Visual Information Processing
A practical driver assessment may be helpful in assessing the ability to process visual information.

Progressive Eye Conditions
A category of eye disorders that worsen over time, potentially affecting driving ability and requiring future restrictions.

Cataract
An example of a progressive eye condition mentioned in the text.

Optic Neuropathy
An example of a progressive eye condition mentioned in the text.

Diabetic Retinopathy
An example of a progressive eye condition mentioned in the text.

Macular Degeneration
An example of a progressive eye condition mentioned in the text.<SEP>A progressive eye condition that is more common in older people and requires regular monitoring for driving.

Retinitis Pigmentosa
An example of a progressive eye condition mentioned in the text.

Blindness and Low Vision Services
Services that patients with progressive eye conditions may need to engage with for adaptation.

Vision
The ability to see, including visual acuity and visual fields, which is essential for operating a motor vehicle.<SEP>The ability to see, which declines with normal ageing and is a key factor in assessing fitness to drive.<SEP>The visual capability of an individual, measured by acuity ratios such as 6/18 or 6/9.

Eye Disorders
Conditions affecting vision that can diminish a person's ability to drive safely.

Motor Vehicle
A vehicle used for transportation, requiring good vision to operate safely.

Peripheral Vision
Side vision that assists drivers in being aware of the total driving environment and detecting objects outside the direct line of vision.

Person
An individual operating a motor vehicle, whose ability to drive safely depends on their vision.<SEP>An individual assessed for eligibility to hold an unconditional licence based on visual acuity standards.<SEP>An individual who is assessed for fitness to hold a specific type of license.<SEP>An individual who is assessed for fitness to hold a driving licence based on visual conditions.

Traffic Stream
A group of vehicles moving together on a road, requiring careful merging into.

Pedestrians
People walking on or near roads, which drivers must detect to ensure safety.

Warning Signs
Signs placed along roads to alert drivers of potential hazards or changes in road conditions.

Motor Vehicle Operation
Good vision is essential for operating a motor vehicle safely.

Driving Ability
Marked loss of visual acuity or visual fields diminishes a person's ability to drive safely and detect hazards.

Driving Environment Awareness
Peripheral vision assists drivers in being aware of the total driving environment and detecting objects to the side.

Driver Awareness
Vision defects can develop slowly, causing drivers to be unaware of their reduced abilities, particularly in relation to peripheral vision.

Vision Defects
Vision defects can develop slowly, causing drivers to be unaware of their reduced abilities, particularly in relation to peripheral vision.

Hazard Detection
Loss of visual acuity reduces the ability to detect other vehicles, pedestrians, and warning signs.

Visual Acuity Loss
Loss of visual acuity reduces the ability to detect other vehicles, pedestrians, and warning signs.

Ageing
The natural process of growing older, associated with the decline in vision.

Older People
Individuals in the older age group, for whom vision decline is an important consideration regarding driving.

Cognition
Mental processes such as thinking and memory, considered alongside vision when assessing older drivers.

Sensory-Motor Function
The coordination of sensory input with motor output, relevant to driving safety in older adults.

Cataracts
A progressive eye condition that is more common in older people and requires regular monitoring for driving.

Conditional Licences
Driving permits with specific restrictions imposed due to diagnosed eye conditions.

Diabetes
A medical condition requiring monitoring for end-organ effects such as retinopathy, which impacts driving fitness.

Retinopathy
An end-organ effect of diabetes that affects the eyes and must be screened for in drivers.

Neurological Conditions
Medical conditions affecting the nervous system, including stroke, which require integrated assessment for driving.<SEP>Conditions that may affect vision, referenced in section 6.3 as other neurological and neurodevelopmental conditions.

Diabetes Mellitus
A condition that may affect vision, referenced in section 3.

Older Drivers
Individuals whose age-related changes may affect vision, referenced in Part A section 2.2.7.

Colour Vision
A visual capability involving the perception of color, which is currently lacking a standardized requirement for drivers.

Doctors
Medical professionals responsible for advising drivers on the implications of significant color vision deficiency.

Optometrists
Eye care specialists who should advise drivers regarding how color vision deficiency affects their ability to respond to signal lights.

Ophthalmologists
Medical doctors specializing in the eye and its associated structures, tasked with advising drivers on driving adaptations.

Signal Lights
Traffic or road lighting devices that drivers must respond to, potentially affected by color vision deficiencies.

Normal Road Rules and Conditions
The standard regulatory framework and environmental circumstances within which the current driving standards apply.

Risk Assessment
A process used to justify implementing a color vision requirement for specific driving tasks based on potential hazards.

Better Eye
The eye with superior visual acuity among a pair, used as a reference point for assessing fitness.

Either Eye
Refers to any of the two eyes when evaluating uncorrected visual acuity against specific thresholds.

Six over Nine
A visual acuity measurement standard represented as 6/9, indicating a threshold for fitness.

Six over Eighteen
A visual acuity measurement standard represented as 6/18, indicating a lower threshold for fitness.

Corrective Lenses
Eyewear used to improve vision, which may be required to meet the standard for a conditional license.

Driving Task
The authority takes into account the nature of the driving task when evaluating applicants.

Underlying Disorder
The authority considers the nature of any underlying disorder affecting the applicant's vision.

Monocular Person
A person who is monocular is not fit to hold an unconditional licence.

Physiological Diplopia
A specific type of diplopia that is considered normal or expected in certain contexts and does not disqualify a person from holding a licence.

Central Fixation
The point of focus in the visual field used as a reference for measuring the extent of diplopia.
